name: Robert F. Kennedy
role: U.S. attorney general (1961-1964) and senator from New York (1965-1968)
summary: Kennedy was a Democratic liberal who enforced civil rights as attorney general, fought organised crime and the Teamsters, and as senator focused on poverty, community development, gun control and ending the Vietnam War. He was strongly anti-communist yet insisted on individual liberty, nonviolence and equal rights, and in 1968 criticised material growth as a measure of national worth.

person-over-state.rationale: In the 1966 Cape Town address he said the individual is the "touchstone of value" and that "all society, all groups and states exist for that person's benefit", and rejected treating any people as "expendable" for theory or policy.

equal-moral-worth.rationale: Said "we must recognize the full human equality of all of our people before God, before the law, and in the councils of government", because it is "the right thing to do".

correct-racial-injustice.rationale: Called for assuring "full opportunity to millions of Negro Americans", said laws alone cannot undo the heritage of centuries of discrimination, and as attorney general expanded the Civil Rights Division and enforced school and bus desegregation.

racial-segregation-law.rationale: Enforced desegregation as attorney general (Ole Miss, ICC bus rules, Prince Edward County) saying the 1954 Brown decision "was right", and in Cape Town condemned apartheid.

total-state.rationale: Said he was "unalterably opposed to communism because it exalts the State over the individual and over the family".

party-controls-media.rationale: Named lack of freedom of speech, protest, religion and the press as the mark of totalitarian regimes and called freedom of speech the first element of liberty.

suppress-opposition.rationale: Defended the right of protest and speech, said denial of freedom strengthens communism, and urged enlarging rather than restricting individual freedoms.

consent-of-governed.rationale: Said government must answer "to all of the people" and referred approvingly to "government by the consent of the governed, as in our own Constitution".

entrenched-bill-of-rights.rationale: Said even government by consent must be limited in its power to act against its people, with no arbitrary penalties, citing the Constitution as the model.

participatory-democracy.rationale: Said freedom of speech goes "hand in hand with the power to be heard, to share in the decisions of government which shape men's lives"; his Bedford-Stuyvesant project was built around community involvement.

positive-liberty.rationale: Said family, work, education and a place to rear children all depend on government decisions and that liberty includes no restriction on seeking education or work; spoke of equality of opportunity "in fact".

national-self-determination.rationale: Described the world he wanted as "a world of independent nations, moving toward international community", each protecting basic freedoms.

national-mission.rationale: Said "the precise solutions of the United States can neither be dictated nor transplanted to others", though all nations should move toward freedom.

rich-countries-aid-poor.rationale: Said developing nations are "gambling their progress" on the West meeting "our responsibilities to them to help them overcome their poverty".

nation-first.rationale: Said that to lead abroad the US must meet "our responsibilities to mankind", and in 1968 warned of forfeiting the world's respect and security through single-minded pursuit of its own goals.

totalitarianisms-equivalent.rationale: Linked differences with Nazi Germany and with communism to the same lack of individual freedoms and called communism a "totalitarian regime", while also saying he was opposed to communism; he did not equate them explicitly.

one-party-rule.rationale: Inferred: from his statement that communism's lack of free speech, protest, religion and press is characteristic of a totalitarian regime.

defeat-communism.rationale: Said he was "unalterably opposed to communism" and said reform is not communism, but also negotiated with the Soviets in 1962, backed a coalition government for Vietnam and in 1967 called the view that the war was to end communism "immoral".

political-violence-never.rationale: Said "what has violence ever accomplished?", that no wrongs are righted by riots and that violence breeds violence; he did not say it is never justified.

revolution-justified.rationale: Endorsed Lincoln's line that there is no successful appeal from ballot to bullet and said the US is committed to "peaceful and nonviolent change"; used "revolutionary world" only descriptively.

limit-guns.rationale: Co-sponsored the 1965 mail-order gun bill and in 1968 said guns should be kept from criminals, the mentally ill and minors; did not call for banning guns generally.

death-penalty.rationale: 1968 campaign reports say he expressed strong willingness to support a bill abolishing the death penalty; the source is flagged as weak.

surveillance-ok.rationale: As attorney general he authorised limited FBI wiretaps of Martin Luther King Jr. in 1963 over suspected communist associates, and backed wiretap laws against organised crime; contested and not about terrorism.

unions-good.rationale: Worked closely with Walter Reuther and Cesar Chavez, backed the farmworkers' union drive at the 1966 Delano hearings, while the McClellan committee targeted union corruption.

priority-to-poor.rationale: Called ending "the disgrace of this other America" an urgent national priority, spoke of the "violence of institutions" against the poor, and made poverty his main Senate cause.

consumerism-harmful.rationale: Said America had "surrendered personal excellence and community values in the mere accumulation of material things" and that GNP "measures everything in short, except that which makes life worthwhile".

spiritual-nature.rationale: Said that even after ending material poverty there is a greater task, to confront "the poverty of satisfaction - purpose and dignity"; described as deeply Catholic in his public life.

noblesse-oblige.rationale: Told privileged students the temptation of comfort should be resisted in favor of building a new society, and answered a question about paying for programs to medical students with "from you".

decide-locally.rationale: His 1968 platform included decentralization of power, and he held that fundamental change comes best at community level, as in the Bedford-Stuyvesant corporation.

tax-the-wealthy.rationale: Argued for closing tax loopholes and told prosperous medical students that paying for his programs would come "from you"; no stated rate proposal.

cut-welfare.rationale: Said welfare and housing programs ignore the causes of dependence and bog down in bureaucracy, but sought to replace them with jobs and community programs, not to cut aid to the poor.

limit-growth.rationale: Called for "constantly accelerating economic progress" as a means to free human capacity, while criticizing GNP as a measure.

arms-reduction.rationale: Urged a no-first-use pledge on nuclear weapons in 1966, criticized lavishing wealth on armaments, and listed nuclear warheads among what GNP counts.

minority-language-support.rationale: Amended the 1965 Voting Rights Act to protect Spanish-speaking, US-educated voters from English literacy tests.

ban-cartels.rationale: As attorney general ordered a grand jury inquiry into collusion and price-fixing by US Steel, though critics called it heavy-handed and it was dropped.

jewish-state-israel.rationale: As a 1948 reporter predicted the US would look to a Jewish state and praised the Jews he met; Wikipedia ties his assassination to his support of Israel. No explicit statement of a right.

state-harmful.rationale: Used federal power for civil rights and anti-poverty programs and proposed new government programs in 1968.

night-watchman-state.rationale: Backed large federal action on civil rights, poverty, housing and education, and sponsored the Special Impact Program.

public-ownership.rationale: Inferred: from his repeated plans to use private-sector incentives (tax credits, Bedford-Stuyvesant), and his saying community action and private enterprise should combine, rather than public ownership.

reason-over-faith.rationale: Said efficiency without ideals leads to Auschwitz and that faith, passion and belief are forces "more powerful than all of the calculations of our economists or of our generals".

notes: This is Senator Robert F. Kennedy (1925-1968), not his son. Views on Vietnam moved from support of his brother's policies to public opposition by 1966-68; the most recent position (negotiation, bombing halt, no immediate withdrawal) is used. Primary texts at the JFK Library were blocked (403) and the books were unavailable, so many topics remain null.
